$comment: Mutation gate. Each entry deletes one safety control and names the tests that
must go red as a result. A control nothing notices the removal of is either
decorative or untested, and both are worth knowing.
Why this exists as a gate rather than an exercise: this repository's recurring
defect is a check that reports success without having run — an assertion behind
a swallowed TypeError, a test whose guard skipped it, a mutation whose search
string the shell expanded to nothing. Coverage cannot see any of them. Killing
Adding a control here is cheap and the right instinct. `find` must appear
exactly once in the file, so a mutant cannot silently stop applying — the
failure mode that made one of these look like it survived when it had never
A mutant that is expected to hang rather than fail may set `timeoutSeconds`
to override the runner's default budget for its run.
See README.md for the runner's own guards and why hangs count as kills.

mutants.control: An existing directory with no valid receipt view is refused, so files Anvil did not write are never deleted.
A different vendor/gateway/API/environment lineage may never replace an existing bundle directory.
Rollback restores the previous bundle whole, so an interrupted install leaves one complete bundle or the other.
Output deliberately changed after import is not discarded without --replace-derived.
Derived state is verified against the exact digest recorded at approval before it is discarded.
A stale manifest naming files that are neither compiler output nor recognized lifecycle state cannot authorise deleting them.
A preserved lifecycle artifact may not silently overwrite a compiler-owned candidate file.
Attesting a supplied contract over a gateway definition is defined only for WSO2 native lineage.
The recorded public gateway coordinate must be HTTPS.
A gateway URL carrying embedded credentials is refused before it reaches a receipt.
'unscoped' is reserved for lineage whose gateway identity was never proven and cannot be supplied as a real one.
--strict-identity requires an explicit gateway id, because an offline export cannot prove its own control-plane identity.
An override recorded when the digests already match would be a false claim in the receipt, so it is refused.
A locked entrypoint absent from its own source manifest establishes no lineage.
Anvil will not infer which of several embedded definitions is authoritative; route compatibility is not byte lineage.
An operator's runtime-coordinate attestation supersedes the missing-coordinate warning rather than sitting beside it.
Path parameters are positional, so /t/{id} and /t/{thingId} are the same route; without this the route-set attestation reports false differences.
A non-regular filesystem node is refused before it is read. readFileSync on a FIFO blocks forever, so this is a liveness boundary as much as a correctness one.
mutants.$timeout: This mutant does not fail, it hangs, so the runner's timeout is what kills it. 45s rather than the 180s default: the honest run of this set takes ~11s on a CI runner, so 45s is 4x headroom against contention while keeping the one deliberate hang from dominating the gate's wall clock (it was 3m01s of a 4m09s run).

mutants.control: A generated SDK refuses a confirmation-gated operation locally, before anything reaches the wire.
A generated SDK refuses a mutation whose contract requires an idempotency key Anvil cannot derive.
Certification refuses an SDK manifest whose confirmation, human-approval, idempotency, or retry flags differ from AIR.
The observed-reality lane drives reads only; a mutation is never sent to a customer's running system, whatever the config lists.
A read may only claim that an operation the application does not serve is gone; recorded traffic's high reliability must not launder a claim the observation never earned.
A Postman request dropped because its (path, method) is already taken is reported, never lost silently.
An adopted MCP tool without a readOnlyHint is a non-idempotent mutation that confirms — unknown side effect beats assumed safety.

The runtime refuses an operation whose wire protocol it cannot speak. Without it a SOAP/GraphQL/gRPC operation is posted as JSON to a coordinate Anvil invented — a well-formed lie, indistinguishable on the wire from a real request.
Each non-REST source kind maps to the protocol it actually speaks. Collapsing wsdl to http_json is exactly the conflation this module exists to end: a source format is not a wire protocol.

Certification refuses a bundle whose wire protocol the runtime cannot speak. Without it a SOAP bundle with servers: [] certifies with zero failures, because every hermetic lane compares the bundle against a mock generated from the same AIR.
The compiler says at compile time what the runtime and certification will refuse later, so an unexecutable transport is not first heard about at deploy.
mutants.replace: const wire = { ok: true } as ReturnType<typeof wireExecutability>;

mutants.control: The endpoint a WSDL declares in <soap:address> reaches AIR. Dropping it made service.servers empty and the generated skill state, falsely, that the source declares no server URL.

The generated clients refuse an operation whose wire protocol they cannot speak. The SDKs do not go through the runtime's executor, so a gate that lived only there would leave four surfaces free to send the lie.
Certification checks the SDK manifest's declared wire protocol against AIR, so a client that believes it speaks HTTP+JSON to a SOAP operation is caught rather than shipped.

A credential carried in the endpoint's query string never reaches the snapshot, the AIR, or anything derived from them. An MCP endpoint's token lives there by convention (Moodle's ?wstoken=), and these artifacts are written to disk and echoed by --json.

A document that compiles to no operations is not the application's contract. Accepting one turns an auth wall or a wrong path into a successful acquisition whose diff reports every operation as removed — a wall of false blocking drift that reads like a real emergency.

A probeReads id this bundle does not define fails the lane. Dropping it silently is how a typo, or an operation renamed out of the bundle, quietly stops covering the endpoint it was added for while CI keeps going green.
A probe that answered with an error fails the lane. The operation was asked and nothing was learned about whether the compiled model matches the application, which is not the same as agreement.
A contract endpoint that was configured but could not be read fails the lane. Not asking is a legitimate posture; asking and getting no answer is a question the operator believes was answered.
The envelope's body element carries the namespace the WSDL declares. An unqualified element is the single commonest reason a real SOAP server rejects an otherwise correct request.
SOAP 1.1 sends the action as its own quoted header; a 1.1 server dispatches on it and answers a missing one with a fault.

A soap:Fault is refused rather than returned as a result. Servers deliver one with HTTP 200 as readily as 500, so the status is not the answer — and reporting one as success would record a failed mutation in the idempotency ledger as completed.
mutants.find: const fault = isFaultAware(codec) ? codec.faultIn(op, res) : undefined;

mutants.control: Only a transport-layer Server fault is transient. An application fault — a rejected transfer, an unknown account — fails identically on retry, and retrying a mutation on one is exactly what the safety contract forbids.

Only document/literal is claimed. An rpc binding wraps the parts in an operation-named element and encoded carries per-element type attributes; neither is implemented, so the compiler records no binding and the transport gate keeps refusing rather than the codec encoding on a guess.

The XML reader refuses DOCTYPE and ENTITY declarations. A DTD is the prerequisite for both external-entity expansion (XXE) and the billion-laughs denial of service; refusing it makes both unparseable rather than defended against.

Certification compares each generated client's declared SOAPAction against AIR. A client that dispatches on the wrong action is refused by the service; one that sends none is refused by a 1.1 server outright.
use="encoded" carries per-element type attributes Anvil does not emit. Refused rather than encoded on a guess.
A message described by type rather than element gives the envelope no body element QName to qualify. Refused rather than invented.
